analysis.investment_thesis: Go Digit trades at 58x earnings and 6.3x book value — more than 4x my Graham Number of ~₹72 — offering no margin of safety whatsoever. With only two full years of meaningful profitability and erratic operating income, this is pure speculation, not investment.
key_strengths: Minimal debt (D/E 0.07) — balance sheet leverage is not the problem here
Revenue compounding at 44% CAGR (₹2,252 Cr → ₹9,716 Cr in 4 years) demonstrates scale
Operating cash flow positive all 5 years (₹1,604 Cr in 2025), unlike net profits
key_risks: Earnings history fails my 5-year test: losses in 2021 (₹-123 Cr) and 2022 (₹-296 Cr), barely breakeven in 2023 (₹36 Cr)
2024 operating income was ₹-269 Cr — net profit of ₹182 Cr was entirely rescued by ₹468 Cr 'other income,' not underwriting
P/E of 58.3 and P/B of 6.28 price in a decade of flawless execution — Mr. Market is intoxicated with optimism
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ ₹72 vs. market price ₹322 — stock trades at 4.5x intrinsic value by my formula
Operating income wildly erratic: -114, -283, +50, -269, +494 — no evidence of durable underwriting profitability
Zero dividend history — shareholders receive no cash return while paying a 6x book premium
Company incorporated only in 2016 — insufficient track record for the intelligent investor
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative standard I have established, Go Digit fails comprehensively. My Graham Number — derived from 2025 EPS of ~₹4.59 and book value per share of ~₹50 — yields approximately ₹72 per share. The market asks ₹322, a 348% premium to intrinsic value. A P/E of 58.3 against my threshold of 15, and a P/B of 6.28 against my threshold of 1.5, confirm there is no margin of safety. I require at least 3–5 consecutive years of positive earnings; this company posted losses in 2021 and 2022 and earned a trivial ₹36 Cr in 2023. True profitability is barely two years old.

What troubles me most is the quality of those profits. In 2024, core operations lost ₹269 Cr (operating income), yet the company reported ₹182 Cr net profit — only because ₹468 Cr of "other income" (investment gains on the float) papered over the underwriting deficit. Insurance companies must profit from underwriting first; investment income is secondary. The 2025 figures look better (₹494 Cr operating income), but one good year after chronic losses does not constitute proven earning power. The intelligent investor does not speculate on whether a young insurer has finally turned the corner — he demands proof, and then demands a discount to that proven value. Here he gets neither.
